title: Ayaz's sheepskin
hook: the king's favorite visits a locked room every day to look at his old sheepskin and shoes (Masnavi 5.1857ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guest house, where every mood is a visitor. Your line was a guest, not the owner. Who came to visit? Day two hundred fifteen.

Some people keep their first paycheck stub in a drawer. Or the name tag from the diner where they waited tables at sixteen. Or a photo of the tiny apartment with the mattress on the floor. They've done well since. But once in a while they take it out and look at it. Not to feel bad. To remember. This week is called guests, and today's story is about a man who kept a secret room, and every day went in alone and locked the door. The courtiers were sure he was hiding treasure. Today: Ayaz's sheepskin.
screen: `THE FIRST PAYCHECK STUB.` → `A SECRET ROOM, LOCKED EVERY DAY.` → `AYAZ'S SHEEPSKIN.`

segments.voice: Ayaz turns up in more than one of Rumi's stories. He was the beloved servant of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, a real king remembered in Persian history and poetry. Ayaz had come to court with nothing, and became the king's trusted companion. In Book Five of the Masnavi, Rumi tells us that Ayaz had a little room, and in it he'd hung up his old rawhide sandals and his sheepskin jacket, the clothes from his poor days. Every day he'd go in, alone, and look at them, and say to himself something like: this is where you came from. Don't get proud. The courtiers noticed. A locked room, visited every day, in secret. They whispered to the king: he's hiding gold in there, stolen treasure. The king trusted Ayaz, but he let them look. So at midnight they broke in with torches, eager to catch him. And they found: a pair of old sandals and a worn sheepskin. That's all. They couldn't believe it. They dug up the floor. They drilled holes in the walls. Nothing. They came back to the king pale and ashamed. There are two ways to hear it. The courtiers are the suspicious mind that assumes everyone is hiding something. And Ayaz, as Rumi reads him, is the soul that remembers its humble origin. Not in shame, but in gratitude. Remembering the old shoes made the fine robes less dangerous. Your line: the old shoes.
screen: `AYAZ, THE KING'S TRUSTED FRIEND.` · `OLD SANDALS AND A SHEEPSKIN.` · `THE COURTIERS DIG AND FIND NOTHING.` · then, large: `THE OLD SHOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember where you came from. Settle, and let an old picture of your life come to mind. A first home, a first job, a hard year, the people who got you through it. Look at it the way Ayaz looked at his sandals. Not with shame, not with pride. Just: this is where I started. Let some gratitude come if it wants to. The bell holds the time.
Ayaz's sheepskin. The king's favorite visits his old sandals and sheepskin every day, and the courtiers who break in to find treasure find only those. Today's word.
Your line: the old shoes. Today, thank one person from your early days, or tell someone the story of where you started. Day two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: In Persian poetry Ayaz is a model of loyal, humble love, and readers of Rumi take his sandals and sheepskin as a picture of remembering one's origins with gratitude.

original.note: Persian: a sheepskin coat, the poor man's jacket Ayaz kept in his room.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man with a secret.
what it means: remembering your humble beginnings keeps success from making you proud.
what a scholar hears: Ayaz and Mahmud, a pair other Persian poets, Attar among them, also wrote about, and Rumi's reading of Ayaz as the soul that remembers its creaturely origin.

notes: Paraphrased from Nicholson: Ayaz's chamber with his rustic sandals (charuq) and sheepskin (pustin), daily visits, courtiers' suspicion of hidden treasure, the king allowing a midnight search, digging the floor and boring the walls, returning ashamed. Confirm each detail, including torches and midnight.
Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni reigned 998–1030; Ayaz was his Turkish slave and later companion and governor. 'Beloved servant' used; confirm the phrasing is apt.
Ayaz's origin as a poor herdsman is implied by the sheepskin and sandals; confirm Rumi presents it so.
The script links back to day 200 ('turned into a Caesar'). Confirm this cross-reference reads well.
